items.bodyEn: Seki is named for the Suzuka Barrier, one of ancient Japan's three great checkpoints, abolished in 789. The Edo post town had two honjin; at its eastern fork stood the first torii of the pilgrim road to Ise. Hiroshige's print shows a lord's party leaving the honjin before dawn. Its old streetscape survives, the best preserved on the whole Tōkaidō.
items.sourceNote: Shoku Nihongi (続日本紀), Enryaku 8 (789); Hiroshige, 'Seki: Honjin hayadachi'

items.bodyEn: 関 is a gate 門 with a bolt inside. The Shuowen Jiezi defines its old form 關 as a piece of wood held across the doors. From the bar came the barrier and checkpoint, 関所, where travelers were stopped, and from things fastened together came 関係, connection, and 関心, interest. Japan trimmed the inner strokes to today's 関.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 關: 以木橫持門戶也; Kanjigen (Gakken)

items.titleEn: 関の山, the Most You Can Do
items.bodyEn: The idiom 関の山, 'the most that can be done', is tied to this very town. Dictionaries trace it to the summer festival of Seki's Yasaka Shrine, whose floats, called 山, were so splendid that nothing finer seemed possible. So 一日十ページが関の山だ means ten pages a day is about your limit, with a shrug of resignation built in.

This station's 〜ごとく and 〜ごとき are two forms of one classical word, ごとし, 'is like'. ごとく modifies verbs (矢のごとく過ぎる), ごとき modifies nouns (氷のごとき目), ごとし ends a sentence. The famous opening of the Heike Monogatari says ただ春の夜の夢のごとし, 'nothing but a spring night's dream'. In speech use ように and ような; keep ごとし for writing and ceremony.
items.ja: ただ{春|はる}の{夜|よ}の{夢|ゆめ}のごとし。
items.kana: ただはるのよのゆめのごとし。
